blocks.text: When an alpha or beta particle is emitted from a radioactive element, it is transformed into another element. Radioactive decay is quite random and follows no symmetry; fluctuations in decay curves are evidence of this randomness. We cannot tell when any particular atom will decay: it could decay immediately or remain unchanged for thousands of years. It is also spontaneous. But in a very large sample the decay follows a consistent pattern when the number of radioactive nuclei is plotted against time (Fig 19.7).

blocks.title: Activity
blocks.text: The activity of a radioactive substance is the number of particles it emits per second (its decay rate). Its SI unit is the becquerel (Bq): 1 Bq = 1 decay per second. The count rate recorded by a radiation detector is proportional to the activity.

blocks.title: Half-life
blocks.text: The half-life of a radioactive sample is the time taken for its activity (or the number of undecayed nuclei) to fall to half of any starting value.

Two conclusions follow. First, no radioactive element ever decays completely, because in each half-life only half of the remaining nuclei decay. Second, the number of atoms decaying in a given period is proportional to the number present at the start of the period. If N atoms are present, the number dN decaying in a short interval dt is proportional to N and dt: dN = -lambda N dt (19.9), where lambda is the decay constant. A large lambda means more atoms decay in a given interval; lambda is the fraction of atoms decaying per unit time, with unit s^-1. The activity is A = dN/dt = -lambda N (19.10); the negative sign shows that N decreases.

If a sample starts with No atoms, after one half-life No/2 remain; after two half-lives (1/2)^2 No; after three, (1/2)^3 No; so after n half-lives N = (1/2)^n No remain. The number that has decayed after n half-lives is No(1 - 1/2^n) (19.11): after the first half-life No/2, after the second 3No/4, after the third 7No/8. Using calculus, N = No e^(-lambda t) (19.12), where No is the initial number of nuclides and N the number undecayed after time t. When N = No/2, t is the half-life: T1/2 = 0.693/lambda (19.13). So if the decay constant is known, the half-life can be found.

blocks.alt: A graph of undecayed nuclei N against time t: a red curve falls from No to No/2 at one half-life, No/4 at two and No/8 at three, with dashed guide lines; small clusters of dots (16, 8, 4, 2) show the halving. Equations: N = No e^(-lambda t); T1/2 = 0.693/lambda; after n half-lives N = No(1/2)^n; activity A = lambda N; 1 Bq = 1 decay per second.
blocks.caption: Radioactive decay and half-life (original graph after Fig 19.7).
blocks.long_description: Every half-life halves whatever is left, so the curve never quite reaches zero. Which particular nuclei decay is random, but the overall curve is very predictable.

blocks.text: Every radioactive element follows this decay curve, but each has a different half-life: uranium-238 has a half-life of 4.5 x 10^9 years and radium-226 has 1620 years, while radon gas has 3.8 days and uranium-239 only 23.5 minutes. Any stable element can also be made radioactive by bombarding it with very high-energy particles, which excite the nuclei and make them unstable; these are artificial radioactive elements.

The half-life of polonium-210 is 140 days. If 1000 atoms of polonium are present initially, how many decay in 280 days? Solution: in the first 140 days 1000/2 = 500 decay, leaving 500; in the next 140 days 500/2 = 250 decay. Total decayed in 280 days = 500 + 250 = 750.

Americium-241 is an artificially produced radioactive element. A sample of mass 5.1 ug has an activity of 5.9 x 10^5 Bq. Find (i) the number of nuclei in the sample, (ii) the decay constant and (iii) the half-life in years. Solution: (i) N = (mass / molar mass) x NA = (5.1 x 10^-6 g / 241 g) x 6.02 x 10^23 = 1.27 x 10^16. (ii) From A = lambda N, lambda = 5.9 x 10^5 s^-1 / 1.27 x 10^16 = 4.65 x 10^-11 s^-1. (iii) T1/2 = 0.693/lambda = 1.49 x 10^10 s = 1.49 x 10^10 / (60 x 60 x 24 x 365) years = 472 years.
